metadata.title: Compile against recent google WebRTC snapshot for ICE support

issue_payload.body:
#117 #118 #121 

## Compilation WebRTC (refs/remotes/branch-heads/4180)

Add SteamWebRTC CMake based build scripts.

- Add CMake based WebRTC build scripts (Minimalized for ICE transport).
- Add Abseil-cpp dependency for WebRTC.
- Update travis script to testing steamwebrtc build step.
- Add option to build steamwebrtc as static library.
- Update IceSession for Turn server configuration.
- Add ws2_32, crypt32 dependencies for static OpenSSL library link.
- Update WebRTC's rtc_base/system/arch.h for ppc64le, s390x build.
- Add HAVE_STRCPY_S definition for check strcpy_s

Usage:
```
cmake -DUSE_STEAMWEBRTC=ON .. 
cmake -DUSE_STEAMWEBRTC=ON -DSTEAMWEBRTC_USE_STATIC_LIBS=OFF ..
cmake -DUSE_STEAMWEBRTC=ON -DSTEAMWEBRTC_USE_STATIC_LIBS=ON ..
```

discussion_timeline.author: tycho
discussion_timeline.body:
Please make sure to clean up the commit history for this patch series. Follow the guidelines presented [here](https://github.com/torvalds/subsurface-for-dirk/blob/a48494d2fbed58c751e9b7e8fbff88582f9b2d02/README#L88) and [here](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/v4.17/process/submitting-patches.html#the-canonical-patch-format), in order to write good commit messages. You definitely should squash several of these commits with a rebase as well. The general ordering for commit history in a good pull request is:

1. Any commits to refactor or prepare the existing code base for your changes.
2. Commits implementing your change, including appropriate build system changes (both CMake and Meson, in this project's case).
3. Any additional followup changes/bugfixes (generally these can be squashed into the commits implementing the change after they've received appropriate review).

The Linux kernel project has some [good guidelines](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/v4.17/process/submitting-patches.html#separate-your-changes) on this.

Note as well: for each commit in sequence, the build should *not* break -- as in, a Travis build should be able to succeed at every point in the history.  This is necessary in case a revert of a specific logical change needs to happen in the future.

This contribution policy really helps with long-term code maintenance. For instance, in case something breaks it is helpful to have a clear and concise history in the commit log to help understand what was done, what was intended, and what we can do to fix it.

issue_payload.body:
Pretty straightforward TURN config implementation.

I tested connecting to a test server via a test client app. Both applications are Windows apps. Server was behind a VPN and the firewall was resisting the NAT piercing. Later when i tried with TURN configuration implemented, the connection was success.

discussion_timeline.author: zpostfacto
discussion_timeline.body:
[src/steamnetworkingsockets/clientlib/steamnetworkingsockets_p2p_ice.cpp] Note: This doesn't actually work. :)  Probably need to make sure that a misconfiguration cannot lead to an access violation or leak of any credentials.  Probably just ignore all TURN servers  if the three arrays don't have the same length, rather than asserting.  Or...maybe if the users and passes list is empty, then that's OK, just treat all TURN servers as unauthenticated.  But if either list is not empty, then all the arrays must be the same length?

Or is there a standard syntax used by applications for specifying the configuration of a TURN server in a single string?    Like username@address ?  (Not sure where password would go?)  I suppose any approach has the potential problem: what if your password has a comma in it?
